text: Give one example of a natural phenomenon and one example of a technology involving magnetism. What role does magnetism play in each?
answer: Examples: Earth’s magnetic field shapes auroras; a compass uses a magnet’s response to Earth’s field for navigation. Other examples described in the introduction are acceptable, with an appropriate role.

text: The north-seeking end of a compass points roughly toward geographic north. Does the region near Earth’s geographic North Pole behave like the north or the south pole of a bar magnet? Explain.
answer: Like a south pole: it attracts the compass’s north-seeking pole. Geographic names should not be confused with magnetic polarity.

sources.description: Introduction to Physics - Magnetism - Background - Q1 (updated to LibreTexts version)

text: A bar magnet is cut into two shorter pieces. What magnetic poles would you expect each piece to have? How does this differ from separating positive and negative electric charges?
answer: Each piece has both north and south poles; cutting does not isolate one magnetic pole. Objects with net positive or negative electric charge can be separated.

sources.description: Introduction to Physics - Magnetism - Background - Q3 (updated to LibreTexts version)

text: An unmagnetized iron nail contains magnetic domains. Why does it not necessarily act as a strong magnet? Explain what changes when the nail becomes magnetized and what can happen if it is heated above its Curie temperature.
answer: Differently oriented domains largely cancel. Magnetization favors aligned domains. Above the Curie temperature, thermal disorder destroys ferromagnetic order; previous permanent magnetization is lost. Cooling does not necessarily restore the previous magnetization.

text: A straight wire carries a current toward you, out of the page. Sketch the magnetic field lines around the wire and indicate their direction. What changes if the current reverses?
answer: Concentric circles centered on the wire, counterclockwise viewed from the stated side; reversing current reverses the circulation to clockwise.

sources.description: Introduction to Physics - Magnetic Field - Description - Q2 (updated to LibreTexts version)

text: (a) Describe the magnetic field pattern around a long, straight current-carrying wire. (b) Describe the magnetic field pattern around a single circular current loop. How does it resemble the field of a bar magnet? (c) Describe the magnetic field inside a long solenoid, away from its ends.
answer: (a) Concentric circles centered on the wire in planes perpendicular to it; direction follows right-hand rule 2. (b) A circular loop has a dipole-like field: through its center and returning around the outside, resembling a bar magnet with two faces acting as opposite poles. (c) Nearly uniform and parallel to the axis inside a long solenoid, away from its ends.

A coil rotates in a steady magnetic field and supplies a current to a connected resistor. Explain why a voltage can be induced even though the magnetic field is steady. Where does the energy dissipated in the resistor come from?
answer: Rotation changes the flux through the coil. Mechanical work turning the coil supplies the electrical energy dissipated in the resistor; the steady magnetic field is not a free energy supply.

text: A closed conducting loop is held fixed while the magnetic field through it increases in strength without changing direction. What is the direction of the magnetic field produced by the induced current relative to the applied field? How does your answer change when the applied field decreases instead?
answer: For increasing applied flux, the induced field opposes the applied field; for decreasing flux, it points in the same direction. In both cases it opposes the change, not necessarily the applied field itself.

text: A strong magnet falls through a vertical copper tube much more slowly than it falls through an otherwise similar plastic tube. Copper is not ferromagnetic, but it conducts electricity. Currents induced in the body of a conductor are called eddy currents. (a) Explain why the falling magnet induces currents in the copper tube. (b) Use Lenz’s law to explain why these currents slow the magnet’s fall. (c) As the magnet falls, some of its gravitational potential energy becomes kinetic energy. Where does the rest go?
answer: (a) The moving magnet changes magnetic flux through conducting paths in the tube, inducing voltage and circulating currents by Faraday’s law. (b) Their magnetic effects oppose the flux changes and exert an upward force on the falling magnet. (c) Energy is converted mainly to thermal energy through the electrical resistance of the copper; at terminal speed, kinetic energy is constant and the lost gravitational potential energy goes into heating (neglecting other losses).
